panels:
Mechanistic interpretability aims at causal, algorithm-level accounts of a network: which components compute which intermediate quantities, and how those compose into the output. It differs from attribution methods such as saliency maps, which only say which inputs correlate with an output. Adebayo et al. 2018 showed that some popular saliency methods barely change when model weights are randomized, a reminder that a plausible-looking picture can be uninformative.

The working assumption, argued in Olah et al. 2020 (the Circuits thread), is that networks learn legible features and circuits rather than opaque blobs. That assumption is an empirical bet, not a theorem, and it is tested model by model.

A mechanistic hypothesis is a claim about a causal graph: component X computes quantity q, component Y reads q, and the output depends on it. Good hypotheses are falsifiable by intervention, not just by inspection. Wang et al. 2022 (the indirect object identification circuit in GPT-2 small) proposed three criteria for judging a circuit: faithfulness (the circuit alone reproduces the behavior when the rest is ablated), completeness (removing circuit parts hurts as much as removing the whole), and minimality (every part is needed). Nanda et al. 2023 fully reverse-engineered small transformers doing modular addition, finding Fourier-style trigonometric algorithms, then used that to explain grokking, the delayed jump in test accuracy.

In the toy case, the prompt is a random token sequence such as A B ... A, and the model must output B. The standard test uses sequences of random tokens repeated twice: if loss on the second repeat is far lower than on the first, the model is copying from context. Researchers then locate the responsible heads, check that one head moves information about the previous token and another uses it to look back, and finally ablate or patch them. The prediction is quantitative: copying loss should rise by roughly the amount the circuit explains. If it rises less, other pathways are compensating, which is itself a finding about redundancy.

The safety motivation is that behavioral tests only sample inputs, while a mechanism could in principle predict behavior off-distribution, for example revealing a concealed objective or a shortcut. The honest state of the field is that complete reverse-engineering exists for small, clean tasks and partial pictures exist for frontier models. Coverage is the open problem: even good methods leave unexplained error, and no one can yet certify that an explanation is complete. Treat any interpretability claim as a hypothesis with a stated test, a stated metric, and a stated fraction of behavior explained.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-01.further: Common misconception: interpretability is not one technique but a family (probing, feature dictionaries, patching, circuit tracing, steering) that answer different questions, namely what is represented, what is causally used, and how it is computed. Another is that a readable diagram equals understanding; the standard is predictive and interventional success. Open problems include scaling circuit analysis beyond cherry-picked behaviors, measuring how much of a model's computation an explanation covers, and ruling out interpretability illusions. The later pages in this book build the vocabulary step by step: residual stream, heads, MLPs, features, then the tools that test them.

panels: The whiteboard picture hides the key structural fact: in a transformer the residual stream is an additive, shared linear space. Formally, for a pre-norm transformer, x_{l+1} = x_l + Attn_l(LN(x_l)) + MLP_l(LN(x_l + attn output)), starting at the token embedding and ending at the unembedding. Because every component only adds to the stream, the final logits are a sum of contributions from the embedding and every layer's outputs, passed through a final normalization. Elhage et al. 2021 (A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits) used this to treat the stream as a communication channel with limited bandwidth, rather than a sequence of private layer-to-layer states.

Each component reads with a linear map and writes with a linear map. A head or MLP projects the stream onto some subspace (its input weights), computes, and writes a vector back (its output weights). A later layer can read exactly what an earlier layer wrote, even many layers away, via what Elhage et al. called virtual weights: the product W_in(later) · W_out(earlier). A component can also erase information by writing the negative of an existing direction. Positions interact only through attention, so the stream at token t carries that token's running state, while heads copy information between positions.

Suppose the stream at the final token of 'The Eiffel Tower is in' receives a 'landmark in Paris' contribution from an early MLP, a 'next token is a place name' contribution from another component, and a grammar contribution from a head. A late layer can combine them, and the unembedding converts the summed vector into logits over the vocabulary. Researchers quantify each component's share with direct logit attribution: project a component's output onto the unembedding direction of a candidate token (after accounting for the final normalization). This measures direct effects only; effects mediated through later layers need patching.

Two cautions matter for interpretation. First, the residual stream has no privileged basis: rotating it and counter-rotating all weights leaves the function unchanged, so individual coordinates are not natural units, though training can create a few high-magnitude outlier dimensions. Directions, not coordinates, are the right objects. Second, normalization (LayerNorm or RMSNorm) rescales the stream before each block reads it, and residual norms typically grow with depth, so the same raw write can have a different effect on a block depending on what else is present. Analyses that ignore normalization can mis-attribute influence.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-02.further: Misconceptions: the stream is not a list of labeled slots, and a layer is not obliged to read only the previous layer's output. It is also not a lossless memory; capacity is finite, which is one pressure toward superposition (see the later pages). Related open questions: how models allocate scarce bandwidth, whether some directions act as scratch space that gets overwritten, and how to define a component's contribution when normalization makes the system nonlinear. The next pages open the two kinds of writers, attention heads and MLPs, and later pages treat the directions they write as features.

panels: A single attention head is best viewed as two nearly independent circuits (Elhage et al. 2021). The QK circuit, W_Q W_K^T, decides which source positions a destination token attends to. The OV circuit, W_V W_O, decides what is written to the residual stream from the attended positions. This separation matters: a head can attend strongly to a token yet write almost nothing useful about it, or attend weakly yet write something important. Heads in the same layer operate in parallel and their outputs simply add, so a layer's attention is a sum over h of independent contributions.

The computation is: scores = (x W_Q)(x W_K)^T / sqrt(d_head), then a causal mask, then softmax over source positions to get weights A, then output = Σ_j A_ij (x_j W_V) W_O. The softmax makes weights non-negative and sum to one, so heads often park attention on a harmless token such as the first token when they have nothing to do; Xiao et al. 2023 studied these attention sinks. With rotary position embeddings, positions enter by rotating queries and keys, so the score depends on relative offset. Everything here is learned by gradient descent; nothing in the objective names a role like 'name mover'.

Take 'Mia dropped her bag'. A candidate head would attend from 'her' to 'Mia' and its OV circuit would write a 'female person, singular, named Mia' direction. Verifying that needs separate evidence: does the attention pattern concentrate on 'Mia' across many such sentences, what does the OV matrix write (examine its effect on the unembedding or on later components), and does patching that head's output from a sentence about 'Tom' change the pronoun-related predictions? Wang et al. 2022 found name-moving heads of this type in GPT-2 small for a different task, and also found backup heads that take over when they are removed.

Attention weights are a visualization of a mixing coefficient, not an explanation. Jain and Wallace 2019 showed that attention weights can disagree with gradient-based importance and that very different weight patterns can give the same output, while Wiegreffe and Pinter 2019 argued the answer depends on what you mean by explanation; Kobayashi et al. 2020 showed that weights should be combined with value-vector norms to judge actual influence. The robust workflow is to inspect the pattern, identify the OV effect, then test with ablation or patching on the head's output.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-03.further: Misconceptions: high attention does not equal importance, heads do not each have one clean job (many are polysemantic in what they do), and a head's role can change with context. Open problems: attention superposition, where many head-like functions share few physical heads (a topic under study in recent circuit work); understanding QK circuits, which the later attribution-graph methods typically hold fixed rather than explain; and how multi-query or grouped-query attention designs change the picture. Connections within this book: heads write into the residual stream, they are the movers in induction circuits, and they are ablated or patched to test claims.

panels: The MLP block is applied independently to each token position, so, unlike attention, it never moves information between tokens. It still holds most of a transformer's parameters, roughly two thirds in a standard design because the hidden layer is wider than the stream (often 4x). Its role in the stream view: read the current token's state, compute a nonlinear function of it, and write the result back. Because positions do not interact inside the MLP, any cross-token reasoning must come from attention writing the needed information into the stream first.

The classic form is MLP(x) = W_out · σ(W_in · LN(x) + b), with σ such as GELU. Many modern models use gating, for example SwiGLU (Shazeer 2020): (swish(x W_gate) ⊙ (x W_up)) W_down, where ⊙ is elementwise multiplication. The nonlinearity is essential: without it the block would be a single linear map and could add no computation beyond what attention and the residual stream already provide. Geva et al. 2021 proposed reading the rows of W_in as keys that pattern-match the input and the columns of W_out as values that get written when a key fires, a useful but approximate key-value memory view.

Meng et al. 2022 (ROME) used causal tracing: corrupt the subject tokens of a prompt like 'The Eiffel Tower is located in', then restore clean activations at one layer and position at a time. Recovery was strongest at mid-layer MLPs at the last subject token, suggesting those MLPs help retrieve attributes of the subject. Geva et al. 2023 described a broader pipeline: early MLPs enrich the subject token with attributes, and later attention heads extract the relevant attribute to the final position. So the place clue lives in the MLP, but retrieval also needs attention.

Two cautions. A neuron is one coordinate in the hidden layer; because the activation function acts elementwise, that basis is somewhat privileged, yet individual neurons are often polysemantic (see page 7), so 'the Paris neuron' stories are risky. Dai et al. 2022 proposed 'knowledge neurons' with attribution methods, and later replication work suggests such localization is sensitive to the method and to the edit being tested. Also, late-layer MLPs do jobs besides storing facts, such as calibrating or suppressing token predictions (Gurnee et al. 2024 describe prediction and suppression neurons in GPT-2).
ai-safety-04-interpretability-04.further: Misconceptions: 'MLPs store facts and attention routes' is a useful first sketch but a simplification; facts are distributed, and editing one MLP often has side effects. Open problems include how knowledge is organized across layers, why wide MLPs end up in superposition (hidden units fewer than features), and how to describe MLP computation in a basis of interpretable features rather than neurons, the motivation for transcoders on page 11. Connections: MLPs write to the residual stream like heads do, and their outputs are what sparse autoencoders and transcoders try to decompose.

panels: The word feature is used in at least three ways. Elhage et al. 2022 (Toy Models of Superposition) framed it informally as a property of the input that a sufficiently large network would devote a neuron to representing. Operationally, current practice defines a feature as a direction in activation space, or a latent unit of a learned dictionary such as a sparse autoencoder, that fires on a coherent set of inputs. A third meaning, common in older work, is any decodable property. These are not interchangeable, so a claim about 'a feature' should say which definition and which method found it.

The usual picture is additive: an activation vector is approximately a sparse, non-negative combination of feature directions, x ≈ Σ_i f_i · d_i, where f_i is how strongly feature i is present and d_i is its direction. The dictionary can have far more directions than the space has dimensions, with only a few active per input. Alternatives exist: features might be nonlinear manifolds, circles or higher-dimensional shapes (Engels et al. 2024 found circular representations for days of the week), or multi-dimensional subspaces. Which picture holds is an empirical question, and results differ across concepts.

A bridge feature is a hypothesis with a standard test protocol. Collect top-activating examples, but also sample examples across the activation range, since the top few can mislead. Check negative cases: texts about bridges that do not fire it, texts that fire it without bridges. Look at the feature's output effect, for example how its decoder direction shifts logits. Then intervene: clamp it high or suppress it, and see whether bridge-related behavior changes. Templeton et al. 2024 did this at scale with a Golden Gate Bridge feature in Claude 3 Sonnet, where amplifying it made the model bring up the bridge in unrelated answers.

Labels are lossy summaries written by people or by an automated labeler (Bills et al. 2023 used a language model to propose and score explanations by how well they simulate real activations). A feature can be broader or narrower than its label, can split into finer features as dictionaries grow, and can fire for reasons the labeler never saw. Activation tells you association; only intervention shows influence. Even a causally active feature can be one of several redundant routes. Good practice reports the label, the evidence it was checked against, and the effect of intervening.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-05.further: Misconceptions: a feature is not the same as a neuron, not guaranteed to match a human concept, and not a unit the model necessarily 'uses' as a discrete symbol. Open problems: there is no agreed ground truth for what the right features are, so dictionary quality is judged indirectly (reconstruction, interpretability scores, downstream causal tests). Different training runs can find overlapping but non-identical feature sets. Within this book, features are the connective tissue: polysemanticity and superposition explain why neurons fail, SAEs extract features, and circuits and attribution graphs wire features together.

panels: The oldest well-known evidence is word embeddings: Mikolov et al. 2013 observed that vector(king) - vector(man) + vector(woman) lands near vector(queen), meaning a relation such as gender corresponds roughly to a consistent offset. The linear representation hypothesis extends the idea to the internal activations of large language models: a concept c is represented by a direction v_c (or low-dimensional subspace), and the degree to which an input expresses c is the projection h · v_c. Park et al. 2023 formalized several senses of linearity (in output space, in input space, and for probing) and argued they can be unified with a particular causal inner product.

Two kinds of evidence are needed, and they differ. Reading: train a probe, h → concept label, and show it works on held-out data. Writing: add or subtract a multiple of the direction, h' = h + α·v_c, and show behavior shifts in the predicted way. Nanda et al. 2023 found that Othello-GPT, trained only on move sequences, linearly represents each board square as mine, theirs or empty relative to the player, and that editing those directions changes the model's legal-move predictions. That combination of readable and writable is much stronger than either alone.

Picture activation points for sentences about a topic: they scatter, but with a systematic shift along one axis. A probe trained on the axis can classify new sentences, which is the reading test. Pushing activations along the axis and watching outputs change is the writing test. They can disagree: a direction can be perfectly readable yet useless as a lever, because the model's downstream computation never consults it. Conversely a steering vector can change behavior through side effects without being 'the concept'. Reporting both, with controls, avoids conflating a measurement with a mechanism.

The hypothesis is probably true for many concepts and false as a universal law. Engels et al. 2024 (Not All Language Model Features Are Linear) found features with circular geometry, such as days of the week and months, where modular arithmetic is done on a ring. Concepts with many values, compositional relations and continuous quantities may need curved or multi-dimensional structure. Linearity is also partly a methodological bias: linear tools find linear structure, so 'we found a direction' does not rule out richer nonlinear encodings alongside it.

A good test fixes the claim before looking: choose a concept, build matched positive and negative prompts, split into train and held-out sets, and pre-register the metric. For reading, report held-out accuracy against a baseline such as a probe on shuffled labels or on a random-weights model. For writing, sweep the strength α and plot the behavior metric together with a fluency or capability measure, because large α can break the model. Use out-of-distribution prompts (different phrasing, languages, topics) to see whether the direction captures the concept or a surface cue. If readability holds but steering does not, report that honestly.

Check yourself: can you state (1) what the probe's accuracy shows (information is linearly decodable at that layer), (2) what an intervention showing a shift adds (the direction has causal influence on the output), and (3) what neither shows (that the model represents the concept as a unit, or that this direction is the only route)? A common slip is concluding 'the model thinks X' from a probe alone. Another is treating the direction found as unique: other directions with positive correlation often exist, and which one you find depends on the data, the method and the layer.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-06.further: Misconceptions: linear does not mean one neuron, one coordinate, or a clean axis free of other content; it means approximate additivity along some direction, with interference from other features. Open problems: when and why nonlinear or multidimensional structure appears, how to choose among many equally good directions, and how stable directions are across layers and between models. Neighbours in this book: the linear probe page covers reading, steering vectors and RepE cover writing, and superposition explains how many such directions can coexist in limited dimensions.

panels: Polysemanticity is an observation about neurons: a single hidden unit has several distinct, seemingly unrelated top-activating contexts. It was documented in vision models, where a unit in InceptionV1 responded to cat faces, car fronts and cat legs (Olah et al. 2020, Zoom In), and later in language models. It matters because the neuron is the most natural unit to inspect: if neurons were monosemantic, interpretability would amount to labeling them. The difficulty is that a neuron's activation is one number, so the same value can mean different things depending on which input caused it.

Two mechanisms are distinguished. Superposition: the network wants to represent more features than it has neurons or dimensions, so features share coordinates and each neuron picks up several (Elhage et al. 2022). Incidental polysemanticity: even without capacity pressure, random initialization and noise can leave a neuron weakly responsive to extra features, and training does not always clean it up (Lecomte et al. 2023). Architecture also matters; elementwise nonlinearities give neurons a privileged basis, which makes alignment of features with neurons possible, yet no guarantee. Attempts to encourage monosemantic neurons directly, such as softmax linear units (Elhage et al. 2022), gave mixed results.

The cats-numbers-quotes neuron is a deliberately silly illustration; real examples are subtler, for instance a unit active for a particular syntactic context and also a loosely related topic. The standard check is not eyeballing top examples but sampling across the activation range, clustering the contexts, and checking whether the clusters have different downstream effects. If the neuron's output weights push the same logits for each cluster, the units might share a function; if not, they are different features that happen to share a coordinate. Directional effects can be measured by ablating the neuron on each context cluster separately.

Practically, polysemanticity breaks the 'read the neurons' strategy and is a motivation for dictionary methods like sparse autoencoders, which look for directions rather than coordinates. It also warns against two opposite errors: treating a neuron label as a full explanation, and concluding the network is unintelligible. Messy neurons can sit on top of clean features. What it does not show is that interpretability is impossible, or that a given neuron is meaningless; it shows that the neuron is the wrong basis for describing the representation.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-07.further: Misconceptions: polysemantic does not mean random, and it does not by itself prove superposition; other causes exist. Open problems: how much polysemanticity is necessary versus an artifact of training, whether architectures can be designed for cleaner units without losing capability, and how to quantify a neuron's degree of mixing. Within this book, this page sets up the next two: superposition gives the geometric explanation, and monosemanticity names the property that feature-extraction methods try to recover.

panels: The geometry is simple to state. An n-dimensional space has at most n mutually orthogonal directions, but it has many more directions that are nearly orthogonal; by Johnson-Lindenstrauss-style arguments the number grows exponentially in n for a fixed tolerance. If features are sparse (rarely active together), a network can assign each a distinct nearly-orthogonal direction, accept small interference, and represent far more features than dimensions. This is the same logic as compressed sensing: sparse signals can be recovered from fewer measurements than ambient dimension would suggest.

Elhage et al. 2022 (Toy Models of Superposition) studied a small model that compresses n features into m < n dimensions and reconstructs them: x' = ReLU(W^T W x + b), trained with importance-weighted squared error. Findings: when features are dense, the model keeps only the most important ones and ignores the rest; as sparsity increases, it transitions (sharply, like a phase change) into storing extra features as non-orthogonal directions. Two features in one dimension form an antipodal pair; features arrange into regular structures such as pentagons in two dimensions. The ReLU plus a negative bias lets the model clip small interference, which is why a nonlinearity is essential.

In two dimensions, three feature directions at 120 degrees (a 'Mercedes star') have pairwise cosine -1/2. If only feature A is active, the vector points along A and a reader can identify it, since the projections onto B and C are negative and are clipped by a ReLU. If A and B are active together, their sum points at -C's direction, so the reader sees a spurious signal for the opposite of C or confuses the pattern. Interference cost grows with how often features co-occur, which is why sparsity is what makes the scheme profitable.

Evidence in real models is indirect but substantial: sparse autoencoders trained on activations recover many more interpretable directions than there are dimensions (Bricken et al. 2023: thousands of features from a 512-neuron layer), and feature counts keep rising with dictionary size. But it is not a settled, complete theory. Some features seem not to be simple directions (Engels et al. 2024), and attempts to measure superposition in large models depend on the decomposition method used. Related work on 'computation in superposition' asks whether models also compute on features packed together, not only store them.

A fair test of a superposition claim has three parts. First, the capacity claim: show that the layer contains more distinct, causally relevant features than dimensions (for example, by fitting a dictionary and checking that held-out reconstruction and downstream loss stay good with a count above the width). Second, the interference claim: check that errors increase when co-occurring features are active together, as the geometry predicts. Third, the intervention claim: ablate one feature direction and verify the effect is specific, not a diffuse degradation. If these fail, the mixed neuron may have another explanation.

Self-check: can you explain why sparsity is the enabling condition? If features co-occur often, interference terms add up and the scheme loses; if they are rare, the expected cost is small. Can you say what the toy model does not show? It does not show that real networks use exactly regular polytopes, that features are all linear, or that every polysemantic neuron comes from superposition. Distinguish the measured object (a trained toy model's weight geometry, or a dictionary's reconstruction curve) from the inferred story (that the network is trading capacity for interference).
ai-safety-04-interpretability-08.further: Misconceptions: superposition is not noise or a defect; it is a rational compression under sparsity. It also does not mean features are entangled beyond recovery. Open problems include characterizing it in real architectures (attention, multi-layer interactions), whether features obey simple geometry, how superposition interacts with computation, and what the true number of features in a frontier model is. This page connects the earlier ones (polysemantic neurons) to the tools that follow: sparse autoencoders decompose superposed activations, and transcoders do the same for MLP computation.

panels: Monosemanticity is a graded property of a unit (a neuron, direction or dictionary latent): the extent to which its activations correspond to one coherent concept. It is not a binary label, and it is relative to a distribution of inputs and a level of granularity. A unit that fires on 'DNA sequences in uppercase ACGT' is monosemantic at one resolution; at finer resolution it might split by organism or context. The term comes from the contrast with polysemantic neurons, and it is the goal of dictionary-learning approaches that look for units that are cleaner than the raw neurons.

Bricken et al. 2023 (Towards Monosemanticity) trained sparse autoencoders on the MLP activations of a one-layer transformer and argued the learned features were more interpretable than the neurons by several measures: blinded human ratings, automated explanation scoring, and by specificity of the feature's effect on the output logits. A distinctive practice was to examine examples across the whole activation range, not only the maximum, since a feature can look clean at the top and muddy lower down. They also reported that features can be stable across training seeds to a degree, and that they vary with dictionary size.

An extracted feature for, say, legal-document boilerplate might fire strongly on statutes, weakly on contracts, and rarely on casual prose. 'Coherent' does not mean 'sharp': the activation is a continuous quantity, and there are borderline cases. A test is the activation-density breakdown: at each activation bucket, what fraction of examples a human or model judges to match the label? A good feature shows high precision at high activation and degrades gracefully. Its effect on the output can also be examined: if boosting it raises probabilities of tokens consistent with the label, the label gains support.

Feature splitting is the standard complication: as the dictionary grows, one broad feature divides into several narrower ones (Bricken et al. 2023 observed this in their scaled-up dictionaries), and in the opposite direction, narrow features may be absorbed into broader ones in ways that create odd gaps (feature absorption, Chanin et al. 2024). So there is not a single correct feature inventory; there is a family of decompositions at different resolutions. Meaning also depends on what you looked at: unusual contexts can reveal a label was too tidy. Treat labels as hypotheses ready to be revised.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-09.further: Misconceptions: monosemantic does not mean the unit corresponds to a concept humans would name, does not mean it is the model's own unit of computation, and does not mean the labeling is objective. Open problems: principled measures of 'how monosemantic' that do not depend on human labeling, avoiding both splitting and absorption artifacts, and deciding how much granularity is useful. This page is the goal state for the previous two (polysemanticity as the problem, superposition as the cause) and the target for the sparse autoencoder, the tool described on the next page.

panels: The cocktail-party picture is apt: activations are a linear mix of many sparse sources, and an SAE tries to unmix them without being told the sources. It is an instance of dictionary learning. Given activations x ∈ R^d (from a residual stream, MLP output or attention output), it learns an overcomplete set of directions, with m much greater than d, so that each x is explained by few of them. Cunningham et al. 2023 and Bricken et al. 2023 independently applied this to language models, finding that the resulting latents were more interpretable than the neurons.

A standard SAE has an encoder f = ReLU(W_enc (x - b_dec) + b_enc) and a decoder x̂ = W_dec f + b_dec, trained to minimize ||x - x̂||² + λ·||f||₁. The L1 term encourages sparsity but also shrinks active values (shrinkage), which biases reconstructions. Newer variants address this: TopK SAEs keep only the k largest latents (Gao et al. 2024), JumpReLU SAEs use learned thresholds (Rajamanoharan et al. 2024), and gated SAEs separate detecting a feature from estimating its size. Practical issues include dead latents that never fire and the choice of dictionary width.

The pipeline in the diagram is: take a vector from the model, encode into a wide sparse code, decode back. The reconstruction is never exact, and the leftover (x - x̂) is not necessarily noise; it can contain structure the dictionary missed. Standard metrics: L0 (average number of active latents), fraction of variance unexplained, and, more meaningfully, the increase in the model's language-modeling loss when the SAE reconstruction is spliced in place of the original activation. Low L0 and high fidelity trade off against each other, and a dictionary can look sparse while hurting downstream behavior.

Known failure modes: features missed entirely, one concept split across several latents, several concepts merged, and feature absorption, where a general latent fails to fire in cases that a more specific latent covers (Chanin et al. 2024). Reconstruction quality is not a certificate of explanatory faithfulness: two dictionaries with equal loss can carve the space differently, and benchmark suites such as SAEBench (Karvonen et al. 2025) exist because no single metric is adequate. SAEs are trained on a particular activation distribution, so latents can behave differently on unfamiliar inputs.

A rigorous check of a claimed SAE latent has four steps. (1) Held-out examples: do top and mid-range activations match the label on data not used to write the label? (2) Output effect: do its decoder direction's effects on the logits fit the story? (3) Intervention: ablate or amplify the latent while preserving the reconstruction error term, and see whether behavior changes as predicted. (4) Comparison: does a differently trained dictionary (other width, seed or method) find a corresponding feature? Failing (3) means the latent may merely correlate with something relevant.

Self-check. What does a good reconstruction guarantee? Only that the sparse code carries the information needed by the SAE's own measure of error; it does not guarantee that the model uses the code's coordinates as units. What does interpretability of a latent (by looking at examples) guarantee? Only that the label fits the examples seen. What does a successful intervention add? Evidence of causal relevance of that direction in that context. Keep separate the three levels: reconstruct, describe, and causally test. Many disputed claims about SAEs come from mixing them up.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-10.further: Misconceptions: SAEs do not reveal the model's own 'true' features; they give one useful decomposition under a chosen objective. Their features are not guaranteed to be stable across training runs. Open problems: the unexplained residual (the 'dark matter'), better objectives than L1 and reconstruction, evaluating faithfulness without circular reliance on human labels, and whether features are best learned per layer or across layers. Next pages: transcoders and crosscoders change what the dictionary predicts, and circuits and attribution graphs use SAE-like features as nodes.

panels: Both tools build on the sparse-dictionary idea but change what is being predicted. A plain SAE reconstructs a vector from itself (x → x̂). A transcoder instead learns a sparse approximation of a component's input-to-output function, and a crosscoder learns one feature dictionary that reads from, and writes to, activations at several places. The motivation is practical: SAEs describe what is represented, but interpretable circuits need to describe how one representation is turned into the next, and nonlinear components like MLPs obstruct that.

A transcoder (Dunefsky et al. 2024) takes the MLP's input (post-normalization residual) and is trained to predict the MLP's output through a sparse bottleneck: f = ReLU(W_enc x + b), ŷ = W_dec f + b_dec, with a loss comparing ŷ to the real MLP output plus a sparsity penalty. Because the sparse features replace the MLP, the contribution of an earlier feature to a later one factorizes into an input-independent weight product and an input-dependent activation, making it easy to trace. Cross-layer transcoders (Ameisen et al. 2025) extend this so each feature reads at one layer but can write to the outputs of all later layers.

A crosscoder (Lindsey et al. 2024, sparse crosscoders) has latents that share one activation code f but have separate encoder and decoder weights per layer (or per model): it reconstructs several layers' activations jointly, so a feature that persists across layers appears once rather than as many near-duplicates. Applied across a base and a fine-tuned model, the relative norms of a latent's decoder vectors indicate whether it is shared or specific to one model. A large share of latents tend to be shared, and a smaller set are specific, which is the starting point for model diffing.

Limits are concrete. A transcoder is an approximation: if its output error is large or structured, conclusions about the MLP's computation may not carry over to the real MLP, so fidelity must be measured, for example by the loss when it replaces the MLP. Crosscoders trained with L1 can mislabel features as model-specific because of training artifacts; later analyses (for example Minder et al. 2025) reported such sparsity artifacts and proposed fixes. And a shared label across models does not show that the two models compute the same thing from it; only matching downstream effects would.

To test a transcoder claim, replace the real MLP with the transcoder inside the model and measure the change in next-token loss and in the behavior of interest. Then trace a pathway (feature A at layer l boosts feature B at layer l+1) and verify it by perturbing A in the real model. For a crosscoder claim of 'shared' or 'changed', test with causal interventions in each model separately, using fresh prompts, and check that a feature's decoder direction has similar downstream effect in both. Report the replacement error and which prompts were tested.

Self-check. A transcoder answers 'what sparse function approximates this component?', and its quality is judged by predicting outputs, not reconstructing inputs. A crosscoder answers 'which directions are common or different across layers or models?'. Neither is the component itself; both are models of the model. If a feature has a similar activation pattern in two models, does that prove identical computation? No; it proves a similar response profile, and the next step is to compare effects. Which tool would you reach for to ask how an MLP maps one feature to another? A transcoder.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-11.further: Misconceptions: transcoders are not simply SAEs on the output, and crosscoders do not prove two models share concepts. Open problems: reducing unexplained error so the replacement behaves like the original, handling attention (the replacement approach usually freezes it), and deciding when two features across models count as the same. Connections: the replacement model built from these tools is what circuit tracing and attribution graphs (page 14) rely on, and crosscoder features are the working material for model diffing (page 25).

panels: In the mechanistic sense a circuit is a subgraph of the model's computational graph that implements a specific behavior. Nodes are components (attention heads, MLPs, or features) and edges are the flows between them through the residual stream. The word is borrowed from Olah et al. 2020 (the Circuits thread), who found vision circuits such as curve detectors assembled from edge detectors. The key idea is compositional: a behavior is explained by components with understood roles plus the connections between them, which is more specific than 'the model knows this somewhere'.

Circuit discovery is usually run backward from a metric. Pick a task with clean, repeatable structure (for example, completing sentences like 'When John and Mary went to the store, John gave a drink to' with Mary) and a metric such as the logit difference between the correct and incorrect names. Then use patching or ablation to find which edges matter. Automated methods exist, including ACDC (Conmy et al. 2023), which prunes edges iteratively, and edge attribution patching, a gradient-based approximation. Wang et al. 2022 mapped the indirect-object-identification circuit in GPT-2 small, with about two dozen heads in several functional groups.

A minimal copy circuit has three parts. A previous-token head moves the identity of the preceding token into each position, so the residual at B contains 'A came before me'. A later head forms its query from the current token A, matches keys carrying 'A came before me', and attends to B. Its OV circuit copies B's identity toward the output logits. The path is checkable: you can patch the previous-token head's output and see the match fail, or test the induction head alone on repeated random tokens. This is the pattern that Olsson et al. 2022 call an induction mechanism.

Circuits come with caveats, and Wang et al. 2022 modeled them well. They found backup heads that took over when primary heads were ablated, so removing a part understated its role. Circuits are partial: they explain a specified task distribution, not everything a component does. Different training runs can implement the same function differently; Chughtai et al. 2023 found that small networks learning group composition shared a general representation-theoretic recipe but chose different specific components across runs. And automated discovery methods can give different circuits depending on the metric and the ablation type. A neat diagram is a claim; faithfulness, completeness and minimality tests decide whether to keep it.

A strong circuit test has several components. Faithfulness: run the model with everything outside the proposed circuit ablated (mean-ablated is common) and check the task metric remains close to the full model's. Completeness: remove circuit parts, including in combinations, and check the model degrades as much as the theory predicts, not less. Minimality: confirm every included node matters. Do all of this on held-out prompts with different surface forms. Compare against random circuits of equal size as a baseline. If the circuit performs the task only on templated prompts, the explanation may be narrower than claimed.

Self-check. Ask what each piece of evidence shows. An attention pattern shows where a head looks, not what it writes. A single ablation that hurts performance shows the component can matter, not that it is the main route. A circuit that is faithful on the benchmark shows sufficiency on that distribution, not that it explains the model in general. If a backup path exists, what would ablating the primary path do? It would show a small effect despite being important. Can you describe in plain words the circuit's algorithm and one prediction it makes that you could still falsify? That is the target.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-12.further: Misconceptions: circuits are not neat wiring diagrams read off the weights; they are hypotheses validated by interventions, and models contain redundancy and distributed computation. Open problems: scaling discovery to frontier models, handling superposition (components do many things), defining what 'the same circuit' means across models, and moving from nodes of heads and MLPs to nodes of interpretable features. Connections: induction heads (next page) are the best-studied example, and attribution graphs (page 14) are an attempt to find circuits at the level of sparse features.

panels: Induction heads, characterized by Olsson et al. 2022 (In-context Learning and Induction Heads), implement a fuzzy version of the rule: if the context contains [A][B] earlier and the current token is A, predict B. The identifying behaviors are prefix matching (the head attends to the token after an earlier occurrence of the current token) and copying (its output raises the logit for the attended token). Importantly, this works on sequences the model has never seen, such as random tokens, so it is genuinely in-context rather than memorized, which is why it became a central model of in-context learning.

The mechanism takes two heads in different layers, composing through the residual stream. A previous-token head at an earlier layer writes, at each position, information about the token preceding it. An induction head at a later layer then forms its query from the current token A and matches keys containing 'preceded by A' (K-composition, in Elhage et al. 2021 terminology); the attended position is B, so its OV circuit copies B's identity into the output. In one-layer attention-only models this composition is impossible, which explains why induction heads appear only in models of two or more layers.

On the sequence A B C A the final A has a query that matches the key at position 2 (the B position), because B's residual stream holds 'my previous token is A'. The head attends there and the logit of B rises. The standard diagnostic is cheap: feed a random token sequence repeated twice and measure loss on the second copy. Heads whose attention on the second repeat concentrates on the 'offset by one' token after the earlier match are induction candidates, and ablating them should remove most of the second-copy advantage.

Olsson et al. reported that induction heads form in a relatively sudden phase change during training, at the same time as a drop in the model's in-context learning score (loss at later token positions minus loss at earlier positions). They gave causal evidence by ablation in small models and correlational evidence in larger ones, and they were careful to say the case for large models is weaker. Models also have more abstract induction-style heads and other in-context mechanisms, including function or task vectors (Todd et al. 2023), so induction is a significant piece, not the whole story.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-13.further: Misconceptions: an induction head is not 'in-context learning' itself, and it is not just literal repetition; abstract versions match meaning rather than exact tokens, which is part of why they may support more general behavior. Open problems: how far the small-model causal account extends to frontier models, how induction interacts with other in-context mechanisms, and why the phase change occurs. Connections: this is the standard worked example of a circuit (page 12) using attention heads (page 3) composing through the residual stream (page 2), and a favorite test case for ablation and patching.

panels: Attribution graphs, developed in Anthropic's circuit tracing work (Ameisen et al. 2025, with applications in Lindsey et al. 2025, On the Biology of a Large Language Model), aim to explain a single prompt's output as a directed graph. Nodes are interpretable features (and input tokens, and output logits); an edge records how much one feature's activity directly contributed to another's. Unlike a circuit tied to a task family, the graph is per-prompt: it says what mattered in this particular forward pass. Graphs are pruned to keep the strongest pathways, and humans typically group similar features into supernodes to read them.

The technical trick is a local replacement model. Train cross-layer transcoders that replace each MLP with sparse interpretable features, then freeze the attention patterns and normalization denominators at their values from the original run, and add error nodes so that the replacement model reproduces the original outputs exactly on this prompt. With those fixed, effects between features are linear and can be computed exactly as products of weights and activations, giving edge weights. The cost is that attention is treated as a given: the graph explains how information is moved but not why attention attended there.

Imagine a path: the token 'Dallas' activates a Texas feature, which feeds a feature that promotes 'Austin' as the capital, which then supports the output. Lindsey et al. 2025 reported this kind of two-step reasoning in Claude 3.5 Haiku, plus other findings such as features that appear to plan rhyming words before a poem line begins. Each of these came with perturbation experiments: inhibit the intermediate feature in the actual model and see whether the output changes as the graph predicts. Edge weights are hypotheses; the interventions are the evidence.

Limitations are acknowledged by the authors. The replacement model matches the original only imperfectly, which is represented by error nodes that explain nothing. The graphs omit the attention QK computation, can miss features outside the dictionary, and require manual interpretation and subjective grouping. Only a fraction of prompts yield clear stories. Large graphs can be hard to verify, and interventions on the original model may differ from those on the replacement. So a graph is best seen as a tested model of a computation, with known blind spots, not a transcript of reasoning.

Validate a graph in three stages. Fidelity: report how closely the replacement model reproduces the original's output on the prompt and what share of the final logit is explained by error nodes. Necessity: inhibit the key intermediate feature groups in the original model and check the output changes. Sufficiency: steer an alternative feature in and see whether the output changes as predicted. Then vary the prompt (swap the city, rephrase) and check the graph changes as the mechanism predicts. Stories that only work on the original sentence deserve less trust.

Self-check. What does an edge weight mean? A direct contribution within the replacement model, with attention frozen. What does an intervention result show? Whether the original model's behavior depends on the manipulated feature in that context. What is the graph silent about? Error not captured, attention-pattern formation, and features absent from the dictionary. Why can a pretty path be wrong? A replacement model can be locally faithful while using a different internal route from the true model; interventions on the original model are what discriminate between these. Could you say which claim in a graph you would test first?
ai-safety-04-interpretability-14.further: Misconceptions: a graph is not what the model 'thinks' in a literal sense, and it is not complete. Open problems: explaining attention formation (QK), reducing the error mass, making supernode grouping less subjective, scaling analysis to long contexts and agentic behavior, and comparing graphs across prompts and models systematically. Connections: it combines SAE-like features (page 10), transcoders (page 11) and patching-style validation (page 17); and it is what the circuits idea (page 12) becomes when nodes are features instead of heads.

panels: A probe is a supervised model trained on a frozen network's internal activations to predict a label. Alain and Bengio 2016 used linear classifiers on layers of deep networks to measure how linearly separable class information becomes with depth; probing then became a staple of NLP analysis (surveyed in Belinkov 2022). The linear probe is the simplest case: ŷ = σ(w · a + b) for a binary label, or softmax(W a + b) for several. If a linear map can read the property, the information is explicitly available in a simple form rather than needing a complex decoder to extract it.

Methodology is where probes succeed or fail. Hewitt and Liang 2019 argued that a probe's accuracy conflates what the representation encodes with what the probe can learn, and proposed control tasks (random labels assigned by word type) and selectivity (task accuracy minus control accuracy) to detect probes that merely memorize. Voita and Titov 2020 proposed measuring description length rather than accuracy. Good practice: use held-out data, regularize, compare to baselines such as probing a random-weights model or the raw embeddings, and test on a shifted distribution rather than a random split.

French versus English is an easy property that is probably decodable from nearly all layers, since even token embeddings reveal language. That example shows the main weakness: a high score at any layer only shows the information exists there, and may be inherited from the input. The informative curves are across layers and across distribution shifts. A probe trained on formal text that still works on informal text and across topics is stronger evidence than one validated on a random split from the same dataset, where the probe may rely on spurious cues such as particular words.

Decodability is not use. Elazar et al. 2021 (amnesic probing) addressed this by removing the probed information from the representation, with a method such as iterative nullspace projection (Ravfogel et al. 2020), and measuring whether the model's behavior suffers. Probes have also been used for harder properties; Levinstein and Herrmann 2023 argued that probes trained to find 'truth' may find something else, such as a correlated feature, and generalize poorly. The right conclusion from a probe is 'this information is present and linearly accessible', not 'the model relies on this concept to answer'.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-15.further: Misconceptions: a more powerful probe is not a better probe, because it may compute the property itself, and a null result does not mean the information is absent, only not linearly accessible to that probe. Open problems: causal probing at scale, probes that remain reliable under distribution shift (needed if they are used to monitor deception or other safety-relevant properties), and combining probes with feature dictionaries. Connections: the linear representation hypothesis (page 6) motivates probing; steering and RepE (pages 19-22) test whether a direction can also be used to write, which is the causal complement.

panels: The logit lens, introduced by the pseudonymous researcher nostalgebraist in 2020 on GPT-2, rests on the residual-stream view: each layer adds to a running state, so the state at layer l might already be a rough version of the final answer. If so, reading it with the model's own output machinery should show predictions forming. The lens treats the stream as an iterative refinement process rather than a sequence of unrelated representations, an idea also familiar from earlier work on residual networks.

Mechanically, the logit lens computes logits_l = W_U · LN_final(x_l) for the residual state x_l at layer l, using the unembedding matrix W_U and the final normalization, and takes the softmax. This works well on some models and poorly on others. Belrose et al. 2023 (Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens) trained, for each layer l, an affine map A_l x + b_l so that the lens's output distribution matches the model's final output, minimizing KL(final ‖ lens_l). That corrects systematic mismatch, such as representations at intermediate layers using a slightly different basis from the final layer.

At an early layer the lens might show semantically related or merely frequent tokens, in a middle layer a more specific guess, and in the last layer the answer. Belrose et al. reported that tuned-lens predictions were more accurate and less biased than the raw logit lens across several model families, and that the lens's predictions across depth could be used as features, for example to flag unusual inputs. A related approach, Patchscopes (Ghandeharioun et al. 2024), instead patches a hidden state into a different prompt and lets the model describe it, which can read information the unembedding lens cannot.

What the lens does not show is as important. It reads the state as if the model were about to stop there; the earlier state may be encoded for later layers, not for the final readout, so a poor lens reading does not mean the information is absent. The tuned lens trains a decoder, so part of what you see is a learned map's own contribution, much like a probe. And it shows candidate next-token predictions, not the reasoning that produced them. It is best used to localize when in depth a prediction appears and to compare across prompts, with causal tests such as patching to say why.

A reasonable test pairs the lens with an intervention. Predict from the lens that the correct answer becomes the top token by layer L; then patch or ablate components before L and check the answer shifts or fails later as predicted. Evaluate the lens itself on held-out text by comparing its distribution with the model's final distribution (KL or top-1 agreement) at each depth, and compare with the raw logit lens as a baseline. Keep distinct the questions 'what would the model predict if forced to stop here?' (a lens property) and 'what does the model compute here?' (a mechanism question).

Self-check. Why can a tuned lens beat the logit lens? Because intermediate representations are not required to be in the final readout's basis; an affine translator removes a systematic offset or rotation. Does a good tuned-lens reading prove the information is used by later layers? No; it shows the state is predictive of the output. Does a bad logit lens reading prove the layer holds nothing relevant? No. How could you argue that a lens-revealed intermediate prediction is causal? Intervene on it and show that the final output changes as the lens suggested.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-16.further: Misconceptions: lenses do not transcribe thoughts, and the trajectory of top tokens across layers is not literally a chain of reasoning. Open problems include lenses for models with different architectures, for multi-token and non-token-like content, and for representations that are not about next-token prediction at all. Connections: the lens is a particular linear or affine probe (page 15) applied with the output vocabulary as the label set; it depends on the residual stream view (page 2); and it is typically combined with patching (page 17) to turn observation into evidence.

panels: Activation patching is a causal mediation analysis for neural networks. You choose a behavior, two inputs that differ in a controlled way (clean and corrupted), and a metric. Then you copy an activation from one run into the other at a specific component, layer and token position, and measure how much of the metric moves. It goes back to causal mediation analysis for language models (Vig et al. 2020) and to interchange interventions (Geiger et al.), and it was popularized for transformers by causal tracing in Meng et al. 2022 and by circuit-analysis work.

Two directions matter. Denoising: run on the corrupted input and patch in clean activations; recovery shows the component is sufficient to restore the behavior. Noising: run on the clean input and patch in corrupted activations; degradation shows the component is necessary in that context. They can disagree because of redundancy or interactions. A normalized metric is common: (patched - corrupted) / (clean - corrupted) applied to a quantity such as the logit difference between the correct and incorrect answers. Zhang and Nanda 2023 discuss design choices, such as how to build corruptions and which metric to use, which can change conclusions.

In the Paris/Rome pair, the prompts differ in a single entity ('Mia is in Paris' versus 'Mia is in Rome'), so any activation that differs between runs is a candidate carrier of the location. Patch each layer's residual stream at the city token, then at later positions, and plot recovery against layer and position. Typically information appears at the entity token in earlier layers and then migrates to the final position later, which maps where the model moves the fact. Path patching restricts the intervention to a specific route between two components, and attribution patching approximates all single patches cheaply using gradients.

Interpretation is delicate. A patch that has a large effect shows influence on the metric for this input pair, not that the component 'stores' the fact. Distribution shift: pairing clean activations of one component with corrupted activations elsewhere can create combinations the model never saw, which may behave strangely. Redundancy and self-repair mean single patches understate importance (McGrath et al. 2023 described the Hydra effect, in which later layers compensate for ablated components). The results are sensitive to the corruption chosen, so robust claims repeat the analysis with multiple corruptions and prompt sets.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-17.further: Misconceptions: patching does not locate where something is stored; it measures where a difference can be carried or restored. It also is not a complete method: single patches miss redundancy, and gradient approximations can be inaccurate. Open problems: principled choices of corruption, handling interacting components, and applying patching at the level of SAE features and across long chains of computation. Connections: ablation (next page) removes rather than swaps, circuit discovery (page 12) uses patching to find edges, and attribution graphs (page 14) validate with interventions of this kind.

panels: An ablation replaces a component's output with something neutral and checks how the metric changes. The component can be a head, an MLP, a neuron, a direction or an SAE feature. The causal logic is the same as in lesion studies: if performance drops when a part is removed, the part contributed. The subtlety is that 'removing' has no single meaning in a network; you must decide what the downstream components receive instead, and that choice can matter more than the component.

Common choices: zero ablation sets the activation to 0, which is simple but can push the model off-distribution if 0 is not a typical value; mean ablation replaces it with its average over a reference dataset, removing input-specific information while keeping typical magnitudes; resample ablation substitutes the activation from another random input, preserving realistic structure. Chan et al. 2022 (causal scrubbing) generalized the idea into a test of a whole hypothesis: resample activations in ways the hypothesis says do not matter and check performance is preserved. Directional ablation projects out a single direction from the stream rather than a whole component.

Suppose a tiny model copies tokens with a head H. Zero-ablate H and measure the loss on repeated random-token sequences. If the second-repeat advantage falls, H carries part of the copying. If it barely changes, either H is not needed or another head compensates. Run the same ablation with mean and resample variants and compare. The report should state the intervention (which tensor, which positions, which replacement value), the metric (loss, logit difference or accuracy) and the dataset, since a different combination could give a different answer.

Why single ablations can mislead: backup mechanisms and self-repair. Wang et al. 2022 found backup name-mover heads in GPT-2 small that increased their contribution when primary heads were removed, and McGrath et al. 2023 described the Hydra effect, where later layers adapt. Result: a component can matter a great deal and show a small ablation effect. In the other direction, an unnatural ablation can degrade unrelated functions, giving a large drop that does not reflect the component's normal role. Interpret ablations alongside patching, and consider ablating groups of components.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-18.further: Misconceptions: a null ablation result does not show that a component is useless, and a large drop does not show it 'does' the task, since it might support many tasks. Open problems: choosing ablations that stay on-distribution, handling redundancy systematically (for example ablating sets or paths), and measuring partial or graded contributions. Connections: patching (previous page) is the swap version of the same logic; circuits (page 12) are validated by faithfulness and completeness ablations; and feature clamping (page 21) is an ablation or amplification applied to dictionary features.

panels: Steering is intervention at inference time on the forward computation, leaving weights untouched. The most common form adds a vector to the residual stream at some layer and positions: h_l ← h_l + α·v. Turner et al. 2023 (activation addition, ActAdd) computed v as the difference between activations on two contrasting prompts, such as 'Love' and 'Hate', in GPT-2-XL, and showed it shifted sentiment and topic of generations. The attraction is that it is cheap, reversible and tunable by a single scalar, unlike fine-tuning.

Steering can use different handles: a difference of means between contrasting examples (CAA), a probe's weight vector, a principal component (RepE), an SAE decoder direction (feature steering), or edits to specific attention heads, as in Li et al. 2023 (inference-time intervention) which shifted activations of heads that probes associated with truthfulness. Choices include the layer (mid-depth layers are often most effective), whether to add at every position or only some, the strength α, and whether to re-normalize. The same vector with different α can have qualitatively different effects, from no change to degenerate text.

An example experiment: choose a style direction, then for each held-out prompt generate with α ∈ {0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4} and score the outputs for style with a classifier or judge, while also measuring fluency (perplexity under a reference model) and capability (accuracy on an unrelated benchmark). The plot of target score against collateral damage describes the trade-off. Evaluation must include prompts unlike those used to build the vector; steering often works on near-distribution prompts and fails or flips elsewhere. Report how many prompts were steered successfully, not just examples.

Reliability is a real concern. Tan et al. 2024 evaluated steering vectors across many inputs and found considerable variation: some behaviors steer reliably, but for others the vector's effect differs widely between prompts and sometimes goes the wrong way. Steering can also reduce output quality at high strengths, or alter unrelated behaviors because the direction is entangled with other features. And steering a representation does not make the model 'want' anything; it biases the computation. Treat it as a scientific probe of causal influence and, cautiously, as a control tool, not as a safety guarantee or a truthfulness switch.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-19.further: Misconceptions: steering is not prompting in disguise (the intervention bypasses the text interface, but may be partially replicable by instructions), not permanent, and not specific by default. Open problems include predicting when a direction will steer reliably, composing multiple vectors without interference, steering at the level of features rather than raw directions, and comparing steering to prompting and fine-tuning on equal terms. Connections: the next pages specialize it: CAA builds the vector from contrasts, clamping fixes a feature's level, and RepE, refusal directions and persona vectors apply it to concepts of safety interest.

panels: Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA; Rimsky et al. 2023) builds a steering vector from paired examples that differ in a target behavior. Their setup used multiple-choice prompts where the model could pick an answer displaying the behavior (for example, sycophancy) or its opposite, and the dataset covered several behaviors such as sycophancy, hallucination, refusal and corrigibility in Llama 2 chat models. The core idea is that the difference between the model's internal state when it is about to produce the behavior and when it is about to produce its opposite isolates something causally related to the behavior.

Formally, for a layer L and dataset D of pairs (p, c+, c-), the vector is v = (1/|D|) Σ [ a_L(p, c+) - a_L(p, c-) ], where a_L is the residual-stream activation at the position of the answer token. At inference, add α·v to all positions after the prompt at layer L, where α can be positive (amplify) or negative (suppress). The averaging cancels prompt-specific content and leaves the consistent difference. This is a difference-of-means direction, related to the class-mean difference used in the refusal-direction work and, in a different form, to ActAdd.

Formal versus casual: gather paired outputs that differ only in register, average the layer-L activations for each side, subtract, and scale. Check what the direction shifts: the style should change, ideally without changing the content of answers. Controls matter: use the same prompts with matched length and topic on both sides; otherwise the vector may encode topic or length differences. Compare against a random vector of equal norm and against simply prompting for the style. A good CAA result outperforms the random baseline, generalizes to prompts outside the dataset, and has a sensible dose-response curve as α increases.

What goes wrong: the vector depends on the dataset's quirks (the format of the A/B answers can leak into the direction), on the layer (effects peak at mid-depth and vanish or become erratic elsewhere), and on α. Rimsky et al. reported effects on open-ended generation that were weaker and more behavior-dependent than on the multiple-choice format used to build the vectors, a common pattern. Tan et al. 2024 found large input-to-input variability in steering outcomes. Adding a vector can also lower general quality at large α, so side effects have to be measured, for example on capability benchmarks.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-20.further: Misconceptions: CAA is not learning in the usual sense, since it needs no gradient steps, and the vector is not a faithful representation of the concept, only a useful difference of means. Open problems: whether mean-difference is the best direction (probes, PCA and optimized vectors can differ), how to choose the layer and strength without overfitting, and how to remove the confounds between the contrast pairs. Connections: this is the recipe for the steering page before it, a close cousin of linear probes and RepE's reading vectors, and the basis for refusal and persona directions.

panels: Clamping, as used in Templeton et al. 2024 (Scaling Monosemanticity), sets an SAE feature's activation to a fixed value regardless of what the input would have produced. Suppose a feature i with decoder direction d_i has natural activation f_i on a token. The intervention replaces it with c and writes the change back into the model: x' = x + (c - f_i)·d_i, keeping the rest of the activation, including the reconstruction error, intact. Unlike adding a fixed vector, clamping also removes the feature when set to 0, and holds it constant even if the context would have turned it off.

Scale matters. In their experiments with Claude 3 Sonnet, SAEs with about 1M, 4M and 34M features were trained on a middle-layer residual stream. Clamping selected features to multiples of their typical maximum activation reliably produced behavior consistent with the feature's label. The Golden Gate Bridge feature was the public demonstration, where the model began to relate many prompts to the bridge, and in some cases described itself in those terms. They also tried safety-relevant features (for example, relating to unsafe code or to sycophantic praise), finding that clamping could elicit such behavior, which is evidence of causal relevance.

The bridge experiment is a schematic of the standard test: pick the feature from the dictionary, clamp it at several levels, and compare outputs to the unclamped model on the same prompts. A graded effect that grows with clamp strength supports a causal role. A fair evaluation includes control features of the same activation scale (which should produce unrelated changes or none) and a metric more objective than a quick look, for instance a judge scoring topic relevance on many prompts. The strength at which text degrades indicates how far the intervention pushes the model off-distribution.

Reasons for caution. Strong clamps produce repetitive or odd text because values far above anything seen in training create unfamiliar internal states. A feature is an approximate direction, so changing it also changes correlated features; the result is not a pure concept switch. A feature may be one of several redundant ways the model represents something, so suppressing it may not remove the behavior. And evidence for feature roles drawn from clamping depends on the dictionary and the layer. Use clamping to ask whether a feature is causally sufficient or necessary in context, not as a verified control mechanism.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-21.further: Misconceptions: clamping is not 'turning a concept on' in a human sense; it forces a particular internal coordinate. It is also not a safety method by itself, since removing a feature can leave the behavior reachable through others. Open problems: choosing clamp values principledly, handling feature absorption and splitting (which determine what exactly you suppress), and evaluating specificity at scale. Connections: it depends on SAEs (page 10), is the dictionary-level cousin of steering vectors (page 20), and is a controlled form of ablation (page 18).

panels: Representation engineering (Zou et al. 2023, Representation Engineering: A Top-Down Approach to AI Transparency) takes a top-down stance: instead of starting from neurons or circuits and building up, start from a high-level concept (honesty, power-seeking, an emotion) and look for its representation in the activity of the whole network. The unit of analysis is a population-level pattern, a direction or low-dimensional subspace across many neurons, which the authors compared to cognitive neuroscience approaches that study distributed activity. The paper's practical aim was monitoring and control of behavior, in addition to understanding.

The recipe has two halves. Representation reading, via Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT): build stimuli that elicit the concept (for example, prompts asking the model to be honest or dishonest), record activations at a chosen token, then find a direction that separates the conditions, typically by taking the first principal component of differences between paired activations. Representation control: either add the reading vector during inference, or train with a loss, as in Low-Rank Representation Adaptation (LoRRA), that moves representations in a chosen direction. The related contrast-consistent search (Burns et al. 2022) finds truth-like directions without labels.

For confident versus uncertain wording, you would write matched prompt pairs, collect activations, fit the direction, and then check both halves separately. Reading test: does the projection onto the direction predict confidence on held-out text, in other domains, and in other phrasings? Control test: does adding the vector make outputs sound more confident, and does it change the accuracy or calibration of the answers? These are different claims. A direction that classifies confident-sounding text may reflect style, not the model's actual certainty, which the control test can distinguish if you also measure correctness.

A concept label is a human choice, and RepE reports of an 'honesty' vector should be read as 'a direction that separates these contrastive stimuli', not as a measurement of honesty in an epistemic sense. Levinstein and Herrmann 2023 pointed out that lie-detection probes can fail to generalize and may track confounds. Whether such readers keep working when a model is optimized against them, or when it is deceptive in ways unlike the training stimuli, is open. The strongest case for RepE is as one monitoring signal among others, validated out-of-distribution.

A well-designed validation has layers. Stimulus validity: check the paired stimuli differ only in the target concept, not length, topic or format. Reading validity: report held-out and out-of-domain accuracy, and compare with baselines such as a probe on random labels. Control validity: sweep intervention strength and plot target behavior against capability loss. Specificity: check the intervention does not alter unrelated concepts. Finally, compare to a prompt-only baseline that asks the model to behave the same way; if the baseline matches the effect, the benefit of the internal method needs another argument, such as robustness or cost.

Self-check. A reader asks 'does this state contain information about concept C?'; a controller asks 'does moving along this direction change behavior toward C?'. Passing one does not imply the other. If your honesty direction separates truthful from false statements but steering along it does not make the model truthful, what have you learned? That the model represents something correlated with the label that is not used the way you hoped. What does 'the label honesty' actually refer to in your experiment? Only the contrast in your stimuli, and any extrapolation to the broader concept needs separate evidence.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-22.further: Misconceptions: RepE does not read the model's mind, does not guarantee control, and does not resolve what honesty means for a model. Open problems: robustness when models are adversarial or trained against the reader, confound control in stimulus design, and agreement between reading directions found by different methods. Connections: it combines probes (page 15) for reading and steering (pages 19-20) for control, shares assumptions with the linear representation hypothesis (page 6), and underlies the refusal and persona work on the next pages.

panels: The refusal-direction result (Arditi et al. 2024, Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction) reported that in 13 open-source chat models up to 72B parameters, a single direction in the residual stream accounts for much of the model's refusal behavior on harmful instructions. The finding is notable because refusal is the visible product of safety training. It suggests that this part of safety training installs a fairly low-dimensional, readable and editable mechanism, which has implications for both understanding and for how fragile the behavior may be.

Method: take the mean residual-stream activation at the last token positions of the prompt for a set of harmful instructions and for a set of harmless ones; the refusal direction r is the normalized difference of those means, selected among candidate layers and positions by which one best controls refusal. Two interventions then test causality. Directional ablation, x ← x - (r·x)r at all layers and positions, makes the models comply with many harmful requests. Activation addition of r on harmless prompts makes them refuse. Weight orthogonalization achieves the ablation permanently by projecting r out of weights that write to the stream.

A study of this kind compares refusal rate across conditions on controlled sets: baseline, direction ablated, direction added, and a random direction of matching norm as a control. It reports refusal rates on harmful sets, compliance on harmless sets, and general capability to confirm the intervention does not simply break the model. Responsible presentation uses abstract or harmless prompts to illustrate the effect; the scientific point, that a direction mediates a behavior, does not depend on any harmful content. The projection of a prompt's activation onto r can also serve as a score predicting whether the model will refuse.

Caveats are important. 'A single direction' is a statement about one effective summary in the studied models, not a universal law; later work (for example Wollschläger et al. 2025 and Zhao et al. 2025) qualifies the picture, suggesting refusal draws on multiple directions and context-dependent mechanisms, and that recognizing harmfulness and choosing to refuse can be partly separable. For deployed safety, the finding cuts both ways: it enables monitoring and understanding, but it also shows that for open-weight models refusal can be removed cheaply, consistent with Qi et al. 2023, who showed that fine-tuning can erode safety behavior. Removing refusal does not create or remove a model's dangerous capabilities; it changes whether they are expressed on request.
