ai-safety-04-interpretability-23.further: Misconceptions: a refusal direction is not 'the safety switch', not proof that models understand harm, and not the same as safe behavior; a model can refuse for superficial reasons or fail to refuse harmful requests phrased differently. Open problems: how robust refusal mechanisms are to jailbreaks and fine-tuning, how many independent mechanisms contribute, and whether such directions can support reliable monitoring in deployment. Connections: it is difference-of-means steering (page 20) applied to a safety behavior, tested with ablation (page 18) and addition, and it motivates tamper-resistant safety work covered in other books.

panels: Persona vectors (Chen et al. 2025, Anthropic) are activation-space directions associated with character traits of an assistant, with examples including evil, sycophancy and tendency to hallucinate. The motivation is practical: language models sometimes shift persona unexpectedly, either across a conversation or after fine-tuning on data that does not obviously relate to the trait. If such shifts correspond to movement along a measurable direction, then that direction can serve as a monitoring signal for personality drift, and potentially as a handle to control it.

The pipeline is automated from a natural-language trait description. A model generates contrastive system prompts (one eliciting the trait, one suppressing it), along with evaluation questions. The target model's responses are collected and filtered by an LLM judge so that only clear exhibit/not-exhibit pairs remain. The persona vector is the difference between mean activations over the two sets at a chosen layer. Applications described in the work: measuring how much a prompt or training example pushes along the vector, monitoring a model during deployment, and 'preventative steering', adding the vector during training so the optimizer has less pressure to move that way itself.

To implement the sycophancy example: write system prompts that encourage or discourage flattery, collect replies to the same user questions, filter with a judge, and take the difference of mean activations. A validity check is whether the projection of a held-out response onto the vector correlates with a judge's sycophancy score, and a causal check is whether steering along it increases or decreases flattering responses. Another is whether the projection at the start of a fine-tuning run predicts the trait shift after training, which is the use of the vector as an early-warning signal.

The claims are about measured behavior-linked patterns in specific models, with several limitations. Judge-based labels inherit judge errors. Trait directions overlap with one another and with style, so steering toward one may move others. Results are model-specific and may depend on layer and scale. Most importantly, a trait direction does not show that an AI has a human-like personality, intentions or feelings; 'persona' names a cluster of behavioral tendencies. The interpretation question of what, if anything, such patterns correspond to in the model's own computation remains open and should be kept separate from the engineering utility of monitoring.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-24.further: Misconceptions: persona vectors are not the model's 'self', and a shift along one is not proof of a hidden agenda; it is an indicator of a behavioral tendency that needs checking. Open problems: how well these monitors generalize across fine-tuning types and to adversarially trained models, the relationship between trait directions and the SAE feature view, and whether preventative steering has side effects on capabilities. Connections: it applies the contrast-and-steer recipe (pages 19-20, 22), is evaluated with probes (page 15), and relates to model diffing (next page), which asks what changes inside a model after training.

panels: Model diffing asks what training changed. Typical comparisons are base versus fine-tuned, checkpoint versus checkpoint, or a model before and after a particular dataset was added. The simplest tools compare weights (but weight differences are hard to interpret and not invariant to symmetries), compare behavior, or compare activations on shared inputs. The interpretability version tries to say which learned features or circuits were added, removed or altered, because that can point at the mechanism behind a behavioral change and may help audit models whose training history is only partly known.

Because two models have different bases, a feature in one has no automatic counterpart in the other. Crosscoders (Lindsey et al. 2024) address this by training one dictionary on concatenated activations from both models, with a shared sparse code and model-specific decoders. A latent whose decoder norms are comparable in both models is a shared feature; a latent whose decoder norm is much larger in one model is specific to it. The authors applied this to a base and chat model pair, finding many shared features and some chat-specific ones. Alternatives include training separate SAEs and matching features by decoder-direction similarity or by activation correlations.

Imagine before-and-after models where a refusal-related feature has weakened and a persuasion-related feature has appeared. That is a candidate explanation, not yet a result. Test by clamping or ablating each changed feature in the fine-tuned model and checking whether the behavior difference shrinks, and by checking on fresh prompts. A complementary test is to find prompts where the models disagree, and see whether the changed features are active on exactly those. The behavior comparison and the internal comparison should each be able to fail independently.

Limits: feature matching is hard because dictionaries can split or absorb features differently, and L1-trained crosscoders can produce artifacts that make shared features look model-specific; Minder et al. 2025 reported such sparsity artifacts and proposed remedies. Finding a difference does not establish that it causes the behavior, nor that no un-captured difference does. And the dictionary was trained on a certain distribution, so changes outside it may be invisible. Interpretability-based diffing is being explored for auditing, for example finding what a fine-tune introduced, but is not yet a reliable audit instrument.

A careful diffing study reports: the two models and checkpoints, the dictionary method and its fidelity on each model, how changes were defined (decoder norm ratio, activation difference on shared data), and the controls. Good controls include diffing two models that should be nearly identical (such as two seeds of the same fine-tune) to see how much apparent difference the method produces from noise, and diffing against a model fine-tuned on unrelated data. Then validate causally by intervening on the flagged features, and check the effect on behavior using prompts not used to find the features.

Self-check. What does a shared latent show? That a direction in the joint dictionary reconstructs both models' activations, not that they compute the same thing downstream. What does a model-specific latent show? That the decoder norm differs, which could reflect a real new feature or an artifact of how the loss distributes credit. What does it take to claim a feature caused a behavior change? An intervention in the model that has the behavior. If a difference exists but intervening on it changes nothing, what then? The difference may be a byproduct, or the behavior may be mediated elsewhere.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-25.further: Misconceptions: diffing is not simply comparing weights, and a bigger difference is not a more important one. Open problems: robust cross-model feature matching, scaling to frontier-size models, distinguishing differences that matter for behavior from incidental ones, and using diffing to catch hidden objectives. Marks et al. 2025 (Auditing Language Models for Hidden Objectives) examined auditing teams using interpretability tools and behavioral methods, giving a sense of how such tools may be assessed. Connections: it builds directly on crosscoders (page 11) and SAEs (page 10), and uses the intervention methods of pages 17-21.

panels: Introspection in this context means a causal, privileged connection between a model's internal state and its statements about that state. It is not enough that the model says true things about itself, since it could infer them from its own prior text or from training data about language models. Humans also confabulate: Nisbett and Wilson 1977 argued that people's reports on their own reasoning often reflect plausible theories rather than access. For language models, the related result is that chain-of-thought explanations can be unfaithful, as in Turpin et al. 2023 and Lanham et al. 2023.

The experimental logic is to create ground truth by manipulating the state, so the experimenter knows the answer and the model cannot get it from the text. In Anthropic's concept injection work (Lindsey 2025), a concept vector (for example from contrasting activations about a topic) is added into the residual stream at some layer and strength, while the model is asked whether it detects an injected thought and what it is about. Success requires reporting the injected concept, ideally before it could be inferred from its own output, with low false-positive rate on control trials with no injection. Binder et al. 2024 used a different test: models predicting facts about their own behavior better than other models trained on their behavior could.

A well-run trial set has structure: injected trials at several layers and strengths; matched control trials with no injection; unrelated-concept injections to check specificity; and scoring that separates detecting that something was injected from identifying what. In the reported results, the best-performing configurations detected injected concepts on only a minority of trials, with performance that depended strongly on layer and strength, and many trials failing or producing confabulation. That honest failure rate is part of the scientific picture and should be reported with the successes.

What can be concluded is narrow: there is some evidence of limited, unreliable access to certain internal states under controlled conditions, which differs from a mere ability to produce plausible self-descriptions. What cannot be concluded: that models have consciousness or subjective experience, that their explanations of their own reasoning are faithful, or that introspective reports can be trusted for safety monitoring without verification. Self-reports are also affected by training: models may be trained to answer questions about themselves in particular ways, which complicates attributing any accuracy to internal access.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-26.further: Misconceptions: introspective accuracy on injected concepts says nothing about whether the model has experiences, and a model's stated reason for an answer is not evidence about its computation unless checked. Open problems: separating access from inference in more natural settings, whether introspection improves with scale or training, whether it can be elicited reliably enough to monitor, and how to defend against models that misreport. Connections: this is the counterpart of white-box methods (next page): rather than reading the model from outside, test whether the model can read itself, using the same activation-intervention machinery as steering (pages 19-21).

panels: The distinction is about the access level an analyst has. Black-box: query the model and see outputs (maybe token probabilities). Grey-box: additionally some information such as logits or the model's architecture. White-box: full access to weights, activations and gradients, enabling the intervention methods in this book. Casper et al. 2024 (Black-Box Access Is Insufficient for Rigorous AI Audits) argued that outside auditors with only API access are limited in what they can establish, and that deeper access enables stronger attacks, interpretability, and fine-tuning-based evaluation.

Each regime has its characteristic methods. Black-box: benchmark evaluation, red-teaming, behavioral consistency checks, and statistical tests on outputs. White-box: probing, activation patching, ablation, steering, SAE analysis, and gradient-based attacks. The two interact; gradient-based adversarial suffixes found with white-box access (Zou et al. 2023) were found to transfer to black-box models, and Carlini et al. 2024 showed that even API access can reveal some internals, recovering the embedding projection layer of production models from outputs. The categories are about what the analyst can see, not about how clever the method is.

The same question often has both kinds of test. To ask whether a model has a hidden objective, a black-box analyst can interrogate it with varied prompts and look for inconsistencies; a white-box analyst can train probes or inspect SAE features for the relevant concept. Anthropic's auditing-game study (Marks et al. 2025) had teams look for an implanted objective in a model, some with interpretability tools and some with only behavioral access, as a way to compare what each kind of access achieves. Simple probes have also been found to detect sleeper-agent behavior in controlled settings (MacDiarmid et al. 2024).

Neither type of access settles safety. Behavior is only a sample of possible inputs, and a model may behave well on tests while differing elsewhere; internal methods may not capture the relevant computation, and the labels they produce are interpretations. White-box findings often fail to transfer: a direction or circuit found in one model need not exist, or be in the same place, in another. White-box access also raises operational issues, since open weights allow both audit and misuse. The practical stance is to treat the two as complementary evidence, each with its own failure modes.

A good study states the access level for each claim and what it allows. For a black-box claim: how were prompts sampled, and could the model detect the test? For a white-box claim: is there an intervention, and was it replicated on fresh prompts? Compare methods head to head where possible, using the same task and ground truth, as in auditing games with known implanted flaws. Also test whether the internal finding predicts behavior the black-box tests did not already show; if it does not, the added value of internals is unclear. Report null results for both.

Self-check. Can a black-box test show the model behaves well on the tested distribution? Yes, nothing more. Can a white-box probe show the model internally represents some property? Yes, as decodability, not use. What would show that an internal feature is used? A causal intervention. What could a black-box evaluation catch that an internal method misses? Behavior arising from interactions the internal analysis did not cover. Why does the book end with this contrast? Because the research question is rarely 'which is better' but 'which question does each answer, and what does it leave open'.
ai-safety-04-interpretability-27.further: Misconceptions: white-box does not mean 'understood', and black-box does not mean uninformative; much of safety evaluation is behavioral and likely to remain so. Open problems: designing evaluations where internal and behavioral evidence combine, assessing how much access third-party auditors should get, and learning whether tools validated on small open models transfer to frontier systems that few can inspect. Connections: this closes the interpretability book by linking its intervention tools to evaluation and oversight; later books on evals, red-teaming and control show how behavior-level evidence is gathered.
